before: Go if conditions use bool expressions. Integers and strings are not automatically treated as true or false.
&& skips its right operand when the left is false. || skips the right operand when the left is true.
denominator !=0 comes first. When it is false, the division is not evaluated.
Short-circuiting controls evaluation as well as the final truth value.
Expected output or behavior: true. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Compare two denominator values and identify which expressions actually run. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A Boolean value is true or false. Go needs this kind of value for an if condition. A number or a string alone is not a Boolean condition.
`&&` means both checks must be true. It skips the right check if the left is false. `||` means either check can be true. It skips the right check if the left is true.
The denominator is the number we divide by. `denominator != 0` asks whether it is not zero. Putting that check first can stop division by zero.
Skipping an unneeded check is called short-circuiting. The skipped code does not run.
The screen shows `true`. The denominator is not zero, and 8 / 2 is greater than 2.
Change denominator to 0. Decide whether Go needs to run the division after the first check is false.
